State your OS, Python version, and commit hash in assignment submissions.

sections.title: Idiomatic Data Structures for Data Science
paragraphs: Lists represent ordered sequence streams; dictionaries represent keyed records with fast O(1) hash table lookups. Sets provide constant-time membership testing and deduplication.
List comprehensions and generator expressions allow concise, memory-efficient data filtering and transformations without clumsy nested loops.
bullets: Use dict.get(key, default) to avoid KeyError crashes on messy datasets.
Use enumerate() and zip() for expressive, parallel loop processing.

quiz.prompt: Which Python data structure provides the fastest average time complexity O(1) for membership testing?
quiz.explanation: Sets and dictionary keys utilize hash tables, giving average O(1) lookup times compared to O(N) linear scans in lists.

parts.title: NumPy & Matrix Math
parts.chapter: Week 3: Numerical Python, Broadcasting & Linear Algebra
parts.summary: Understand vectorized execution, memory layout, n-dimensional array manipulation, and broadcasting rules.
parts.objective: Perform multi-dimensional array operations, matrix multiplications, and compute vector norms efficiently.

sections.title: Why Vectorization Dominates Pure Python Loops
paragraphs: Pure Python loops incur heavy dynamic type-checking overhead on every iteration. NumPy delegates array calculations to contiguous C-level memory blocks with SIMD vectorization.
Broadcasting allows NumPy to perform arithmetic on arrays of different shapes without copying data, stretching compatible trailing dimensions automatically.
bullets: Avoid Python for-loops over arrays; use vectorized ufuncs (np.sum, np.mean).
Broadcasting rule: two dimensions are compatible if they are equal, or one of them is 1.

visual.title: NumPy Memory Layout and Broadcasting
visual.caption: CONTIGUOUS MEMORY BUFFER · SIMD OPERATIONS · ZERO-COPY BROADCASTING

unit_vector = [x / l2_norm for x in vector]
print(f"Unit Vector: {unit_vector}, Norm: {sum(x**2 for x in unit_vector)**0.5:.1f}")

parts.title: Data Analysis & EDA
parts.chapter: Week 4: Exploratory Data Analysis with Pandas
parts.summary: Load real-world tabular datasets, handle missing values, inspect distributions, and compute summary statistics.
parts.objective: Conduct comprehensive exploratory data analysis (EDA) and identify data anomalies before modeling.

sections.title: The First Rule of Real-World Data
paragraphs: Real-world data is always messy: missing values, sensor errors, duplicated records, and distribution skews. An algorithm will uncritically fit whatever noise you feed it.
Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) is the discipline of understanding data structure through descriptive statistics and visualizations before training any predictive model.
bullets: Check df.info(), df.describe(), and missing value counts (df.isna().sum()).
Inspect class balance immediately when working with classification tasks.

visual.title: Exploratory Data Analysis Pipeline
visual.caption: RAW CSV · DATA CLEANING · SUMMARY STATS · DISTRIBUTION PLOTS

example.description: Compute interquartile range (IQR) to detect outliers
example.code:
values = [10, 12, 14, 15, 16, 18, 20, 22, 100]
q1 = sorted(values)[len(values) // 4]
q3 = sorted(values)[(len(values) * 3) // 4]
iqr = q3 - q1
upper_fence = q3 + 1.5 * iqr
outliers = [x for x in values if x > upper_fence]
print(f"Q1={q1}, Q3={q3}, IQR={iqr}, Outliers: {outliers}")

parts.title: Data Preprocessing
parts.summary: Prepare raw features for machine learning: categorical encoding, numerical scaling, and missing value strategies.
parts.objective: Transform heterogeneous feature columns into numeric tensors while avoiding data leakage.

sections.title: Teacher's Golden Rule: Split First
paragraphs: Never fit a scaler or imputer on the whole dataset! Information about the test distribution (like test set mean or variance) will contaminate your model, leading to overly optimistic results that fail in production.
Fit your imputer, One-Hot Encoder, and StandardScaler strictly on the training partition, then transform both training and test sets using the fitted parameters.
bullets: One-Hot Encoding for nominal variables (Color: Red, Blue, Green).
Ordinal Encoding for ranked variables (Size: Small, Medium, Large).
Use StandardScaler for models assuming Gaussian inputs (Logistic, SVM, Neural Nets).

visual.title: Preprocessing Without Data Leakage
visual.caption: RAW DATA · TRAIN/TEST SPLIT · FIT ON TRAIN ONLY · TRANSFORM TEST

example.description: Standardize features using training mean and std
example.code:
train_x = [10.0, 20.0, 30.0]
test_x  = [15.0, 25.0]

mu = sum(train_x) / len(train_x)
sigma = (sum((x - mu)**2 for x in train_x) / len(train_x)) ** 0.5

scaled_train = [(x - mu) / sigma for x in train_x]
scaled_test  = [(x - mu) / sigma for x in test_x]
print(f"Train Scaled: {scaled_train}")
print(f"Test Scaled:  {scaled_test}")

exercise.starter:

train_max = 50.0
test_val = 30.0

# Compute min-max scaled value
scaled_val = 0.0
exercise.hint: Subtract train_min from test_val, then divide by (train_max - train_min).

quiz.prompt: Why must you NOT calculate feature mean and standard deviation on the full dataset before splitting?
choices: It causes data leakage by exposing test statistics during training
It makes computation twice as slow
It causes an automatic syntax error
It changes the number of rows in the dataset
quiz.explanation: Calculating normalization parameters on the entire dataset incorporates test-set distribution information into the training pipeline, violating independent held-out evaluation.

parts.title: Supervised Regression
parts.chapter: Week 6: Linear Regression, Cost Functions & Regularization
parts.summary: Understand ordinary least squares, gradient descent optimization, mean squared error, and Ridge/Lasso penalties.
parts.objective: Train and evaluate linear regression models, interpret feature weights, and prevent overfitting with regularization.

sections.title: The Geometry of Linear Prediction
paragraphs: Linear regression predicts a continuous target via a weighted combination of input features plus an intercept: y = w1*x1 + w2*x2 + ... + b.

Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) finds the hyperplane that minimizes the Mean Squared Error (MSE). When features are collinear or numerous, L2 (Ridge) and L1 (Lasso) penalties prevent weights from exploding.
bullets: Ridge (L2): shrinks weights smoothly toward zero, handling multicollinearity.
Lasso (L1): drives non-informative feature weights strictly to zero, performing automated feature selection.
Evaluate using RMSE, MAE, and R² (coefficient of determination).

visual.title: Linear Regression and Loss Surface
visual.caption: HYPERPLANE FIT · RESIDUAL SQUARES · GRADIENT DESCENT UPDATES

example.code:
y_true = [3.0, -0.5, 2.0, 7.0]
y_pred = [2.5,  0.0, 2.0, 8.0]
mse = sum((yt - yp) ** 2 for yt, yp in zip(y_true, y_pred)) / len(y_true)
print(f"MSE: {mse:.4f}, RMSE: {mse**0.5:.4f}")

exercise.solution: mae = sum(abs(yt - yp) for yt, yp in zip(y_true, y_pred)) / len(y_true)

quiz.prompt: Which regularization technique can shrink feature weights to exactly zero, performing feature selection?
quiz.explanation: L1 regularization introduces a diamond-shaped constraint region with sharp corners on feature axes, driving weights of uninformative features strictly to zero.

parts.title: Supervised Classification
parts.chapter: Week 7: Logistic Regression, Decision Trees & Midterm Checkpoint
parts.summary: Master binary classification, the sigmoid function, decision tree splits with Gini impurity, and pass Checkpoint Exam 1.
parts.objective: Train classic classifiers, visualize decision boundaries, and interpret probabilities.

sections.title: From Linear Scores to Probabilities
paragraphs: Logistic regression passes a linear score z through the sigmoid function: σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e^-z), mapping real numbers to [0, 1] as class probabilities.
Decision trees recursively split feature space along orthogonal boundaries to maximize node purity, measured by Gini impurity or Shannon entropy.
bullets: Checkpoint Exam 1 covers Weeks 1 through 7 (20% of your course grade).
Decision Trees require no feature scaling, but are prone to high variance if left unpruned.

visual.title: Linear Boundary vs Tree Partitioning
visual.caption: LOGISTIC SIGMOID BOUNDARY · DECISION TREE AXIS-ALIGNED RECTANGLES

example.description: Calculate Gini Impurity for a binary node
example.code:
p_positive = 0.8
p_negative = 0.2
gini = 1.0 - (p_positive**2 + p_negative**2)
print(f"Node Gini Impurity: {gini:.2f} (Pure node = 0.0, Maximum impurity = 0.5)")

exercise.prompt: Calculate Gini impurity for a split node containing 3 positive instances and 1 negative instance. Store in gini_impurity.
exercise.starter:
pos = 3
neg = 1
total = pos + neg
# Calculate Gini Impurity: 1 - sum(p_i^2)
gini_impurity = 0.0
exercise.solution:
p1 = pos / total
p2 = neg / total
gini_impurity = 1.0 - (p1**2 + p2**2)

quiz.prompt: What is the Gini impurity of a perfectly pure node where all samples belong to the exact same class?
quiz.explanation: If all samples belong to one class, p=1.0 and Gini = 1 - 1.0^2 = 0.0.

parts.title: Advanced Classifiers
parts.chapter: Week 8: Support Vector Machines & K-Nearest Neighbors
parts.summary: Understand margin maximization, the SVM kernel trick, distance metrics, and non-parametric instance-based learning.
parts.objective: Select optimal kernels, tune hyperparameters (C, gamma, k), and evaluate classification boundaries.

sections.title: Maximizing the Margin of Separation
paragraphs: Support Vector Machines find the hyperplane that maximizes the margin (distance) between the closest opposing data points (support vectors).
The Kernel Trick projects non-linearly separable data into higher-dimensional Hilbert spaces without computing coordinates explicitly.
bullets: Always scale features before running SVM and KNN (distance is scale-dependent!).
Choose small k in KNN for flexible boundaries; choose larger k to resist noise.

visual.caption: SUPPORT VECTORS · MARGIN CUSHION · RBF KERNEL PROJECTION

quiz.prompt: Why is feature scaling mandatory before training K-Nearest Neighbors or SVM with RBF kernel?
choices: Unscaled features with large numerical ranges dominate distance calculations
It reduces the number of features automatically
quiz.explanation: Distance calculations rely on coordinate differences; a feature in thousands (like salary) will overwhelm a feature in single digits (like age) unless both are normalized.

parts.title: Model Evaluation & Metrics
parts.chapter: Week 9: Confusion Matrix, ROC-AUC & The 99% Accuracy Trap
parts.summary: Master precision, recall, specificity, F1-score, ROC curves, and cross-validation protocols.
parts.objective: Diagnose classification errors, detect class imbalance traps, and plot ROC curves.

sections.title: Master Teacher Note: The 99% Accuracy Trap
paragraphs: Consider a disease detection task where 99 out of 100 people are healthy, and 1 has the disease. A useless dummy model that simply predicts 'Healthy' for everyone achieves 99% accuracy!
Accuracy is misleading on imbalanced datasets. You must evaluate Precision (how many predicted sick people actually have the disease) and Recall (how many sick people the test successfully detected).
bullets: Precision = TP / (TP + FP) — cost of false alarms.
Recall = TP / (TP + FN) — cost of missed positives.
F1-Score = 2 * (Precision * Recall) / (Precision + Recall).

visual.title: The Four Quadrants of the Confusion Matrix
visual.caption: TRUE POSITIVES · FALSE POSITIVES · TRUE NEGATIVES · FALSE NEGATIVES

example.description: Calculate F1 score from TP, FP, FN
example.code:
tp, fp, fn = 80, 10, 20
prec = tp / (tp + fp)
rec = tp / (tp + fn)
f1 = 2 * prec * rec / (prec + rec)
print(f"Precision: {prec:.1%}, Recall: {rec:.1%}, F1-Score: {f1:.3f}")

exercise.prompt: Calculate Precision and Recall from tp=45, fp=5, fn=15. Store the harmonic mean F1-Score in f1.
exercise.starter:
tp, fp, fn = 45, 5, 15
# Calculate F1-Score
f1 = 0.0
exercise.solution:
prec = tp / (tp + fp)
rec = tp / (tp + fn)
f1 = 2 * (prec * rec) / (prec + rec)

quiz.prompt: In a cancer screening system, which metric should be prioritized to ensure as few malignant tumors as possible are missed?
quiz.explanation: High recall minimizes False Negatives, ensuring that individuals who actually have cancer are not mistakenly sent home.

parts.title: Ensemble Learning
parts.chapter: Week 10: Bagging, Random Forests & Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)
parts.summary: Harness the wisdom of crowds: build bagging ensembles, random forests, and gradient boosted decision trees.
parts.objective: Train and tune XGBoost and Random Forest models on structured tabular benchmarks.

sections.title: The Dominance of Tree Ensembles on Tabular Data
paragraphs: In Kaggle competitions and industry production systems, Gradient Boosted Decision Trees (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost) consistently outperform deep learning on tabular data.
Random Forests train independent trees in parallel on bootstrap samples. Boosting trains trees sequentially, where each new tree fits the residual errors of prior trees.
bullets: Random Forest: variance reduction through bagging and feature subsampling.
Gradient Boosting: bias reduction through iterative gradient descent on loss residuals.
Always tune n_estimators, max_depth, and learning_rate.

visual.title: Bagging vs Boosting Architecture
visual.caption: RANDOM FOREST (PARALLEL VOTING) VS GRADIENT BOOSTING (SEQUENTIAL CORRECTION)

example.code:
tree_preds = [1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1]
ensemble_vote = 1 if tree_preds.count(1) > len(tree_preds) / 2 else 0
confidence = tree_preds.count(ensemble_vote) / len(tree_preds)
print(f"Ensemble Vote: {ensemble_vote} (Agreement: {confidence:.0%})")

quiz.prompt: What is the primary difference in how Random Forests and Gradient Boosted Trees build their ensembles?
choices: Random Forests build trees in parallel; Gradient Boosting builds trees sequentially
Random Forests only work for regression; Boosting only for classification
Random Forests do not use decision trees
Gradient Boosting cannot handle non-linear data
quiz.explanation: Random Forest trains diverse trees independently in parallel; Gradient Boosting builds trees sequentially, where each tree corrects the residual errors of its predecessor.

parts.title: Unsupervised Learning
parts.chapter: Week 11: K-Means Clustering & Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
parts.summary: Discover hidden structures in unlabeled data: Lloyd's algorithm, silhouette scores, and dimensionality reduction.
parts.objective: Segment customer profiles with K-Means and compress high-dimensional feature spaces with PCA.

sections.title: Finding Structure Without Labels
paragraphs: Most data in the real world is unlabeled. Unsupervised learning identifies latent clusters, groupings, and low-dimensional manifolds without human annotations.
K-Means iteratively alternates between assigning points to the nearest centroid and recalculating centroid positions. PCA finds the orthogonal axes of maximum variance to compress dimensions.
bullets: Use the Elbow Method and Silhouette Score to choose cluster count k.
Use PCA to visualize high-dimensional data in 2D or 3D scatter plots.

visual.title: Clustering and Dimensionality Reduction
visual.caption: DISTANCE TO CENTROIDS · CLUSTER ASSIGNMENTS · MAXIMUM VARIANCE PROJECTION

example.description: Calculate Euclidean distance to cluster centroids
example.code:
point = (2.0, 3.0)
centroids = [(1.0, 1.0), (5.0, 5.0)]
distances = [((point[0]-c[0])**2 + (point[1]-c[1])**2)**0.5 for c in centroids]
closest_cluster = distances.index(min(distances))
print(f"Point {point} assigned to Centroid {closest_cluster} (dist={min(distances):.2f})")

quiz.prompt: What does Principal Component Analysis (PCA) preserve when projecting data onto fewer dimensions?
quiz.explanation: PCA identifies orthogonal principal directions that maximize the variance of the projected data points, minimizing reconstruction error.

parts.title: Neural Networks & PyTorch
parts.chapter: Week 12: Deep Learning Foundations & PyTorch Workflows
parts.summary: Build multi-layer perceptrons from scratch: forward pass, activation functions, backpropagation, and PyTorch tensors.
parts.objective: Implement an end-to-end neural network training loop in PyTorch with loss calculation and gradient updates.

sections.title: The Anatomy of a Deep Learning Loop
paragraphs: A neural network is a parameterized function approximator. In PyTorch, every training step follows five sacred lines: (1) forward pass, (2) compute loss, (3) zero gradients, (4) backward pass, and (5) optimizer step.
Activation functions (ReLU, GeLU, Sigmoid) introduce non-linearity. Without them, even a 100-layer neural network collapses into a single linear regression!
bullets: optimizer.zero_grad() prevents gradient accumulation across batches.
loss.backward() executes reverse-mode autodiff through the computation graph.
optimizer.step() updates weights via gradient descent.

visual.title: The PyTorch Training Step
visual.caption: FORWARD PASS · CRITERION LOSS · ZERO GRAD · BACKPROP · OPTIMIZER STEP

example.description: Forward pass of a single neuron with ReLU
example.code:
inputs = [1.5, -2.0, 3.0]
weights = [0.4, 0.8, -0.5]
bias = 0.2
z = sum(w * x for w, x in zip(weights, inputs)) + bias
activation = max(0.0, z) # ReLU
print(f"Pre-activation z: {z:.2f}, Post-activation ReLU: {activation:.2f}")

exercise.prompt: Compute the post-activation output of a neuron using the ReLU function: max(0.0, z), where z = sum(w_i * x_i) + bias. Store in output.
exercise.starter:
x = [2.0, 3.0]
w = [0.5, -1.0]
bias = 1.0
# Compute ReLU output
output = 0.0
exercise.solution:
z = sum(wi * xi for wi, xi in zip(w, x)) + bias
output = max(0.0, z)

quiz.prompt: Why are non-linear activation functions (like ReLU) mandatory in multi-layer neural networks?
choices: Without non-linearities, multiple linear layers collapse mathematically into a single linear transform
They prevent code from running out of memory
They force all weights to become positive
quiz.explanation: The composition of linear functions is always strictly linear: W2*(W1*x) = (W2*W1)*x. Non-linear activations allow networks to approximate arbitrary complex functions.
